## My thinking this year

Well, I'm getting on in years now — 60 — and it's just me and the wife on these 6 mu. Our two boys went off to the city for work years ago, so we can't count on them except maybe at Spring Festival. Twenty years I've been on this land, and I know what works.

Most of my land — four mu — I keep in the cabbage rotation. Spring cabbage comes out first, then I put in Chinese cabbage for fall, then another round of cabbage after that. Cabbage sells steady at the county market and the traders come right to the village when it's ready. I've been doing it this way for maybe eight or nine years now. The other two mu I split — one for chili, one for kidney bean. Chili brings in good cash if prices hold, and kidney bean is easy to grow, doesn't need much fertilizer, and we eat some ourselves and sell the rest dried.

For fertilizer, I do what my neighbor Old Wang does — he gets good cabbage every year. I spread the pig manure we collect over winter, maybe two cartloads per mu, then one bag of compound fertilizer (the 15-15-15 kind) before transplanting. Then when the cabbage starts heading up, I top-dress urea — two times, maybe half a bag each mu each time. For chili I do about the same but a little less urea because too much makes the plants all leaf and no fruit — learned that the hard way about five years back. Kidney bean I barely fertilize, just a little compound at planting. Beans make their own somehow, that's what everyone says.

Water — I've got the well share with three other families. Cabbage needs water, no way around it. I irrigate maybe every week or ten days depending on rain. Costs me money to run the pump though, so I watch the sky.

Pesticide I try to keep low because it's expensive and the vegetable buyers these days sometimes ask. But cabbage worm I have to spray for, and chili gets aphids almost every year. I buy what the agri-supply shop recommends.

I do all the tillage with the rototiller — I don't own one, I hire Little Zhang from the next village, 60 yuan a mu. Transplanting, weeding, harvesting — me and the wife do it all. It's hard on my back now but we manage.

Cash is always tight. Seeds, fertilizer, pesticide, pump electricity, the rototiller fee — adds up fast. I try to keep something in reserve in case something goes wrong.
